paragraphs.text: Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation $\sqrt{20}=4.47$. The total rate estimate has a relative standard deviation of about 22.4%, compared with 100% for one cell. Population averaging helps because the independent count variances add while the mean signal adds directly. If cells share an additional fluctuating drive, that common variation will not disappear in the same way.
paragraphs.reason: The original population paragraph establishes the exact two cases, averaging reason and common-drive limit; it supplies the figure inputs without changing their meaning.

paragraphs.text: Analytic teaching construction for the chapter’s 20 Hz, 50 ms example. The count is Poisson with mean 1 for one cell and mean 20 for 20 conditionally independent cells. Both panels plot the rate per cell $K/(N\Delta t)$, so both estimates have mean 20 Hz; their standard deviations are 20 Hz and 4.47 Hz. Each stem is a probability at one possible estimate, rather than a continuous density. Only estimates through 100 Hz are drawn. The independence condition concerns fixed modeled rates, not complete recurrent spike trains.
paragraphs.reason: Retain: rate normalization, discrete probability versus density, finite drawn range and conditional independence are needed to interpret this actual plot. Numeric repetition lets the caption identify its own model.

paragraphs.text: Two discrete Poisson distributions share a rate per cell axis. One cell has widely spaced possible estimates at zero, twenty, forty hertz and so on, with probability 0.368 at zero. The twenty cell estimate has possible values one hertz apart and clusters around twenty hertz. Their means match, but the rate standard deviation falls from twenty to 4.47 hertz.
paragraphs.reason: Retain: describes support spacing, the zero-count event and matched means for readers who cannot see the stems.

paragraphs.text: Dividing the pooled rate estimate by 20 keeps the expected rate per cell fixed, while independent averaging reduces its relative spread. See [Poisson count likelihood, SI Eq. S43, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9).
paragraphs.reason: Retain: pooled rate estimate makes the division by20 a rate-to-rate operation; it states what normalization changes and preserves.

paragraphs.text: For changing rates, the expected count is the integral $\lambda=\int r(t)\,dt$. In a recurrent network, $r(t)$ itself depends on past activity. The useful independence statement is therefore conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. Averaging over the evolving state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. This qualification prevents treating a recurrent Poisson network as a collection of independent complete spike trains.
paragraphs.reason: The following original paragraph extends fixed rates to changing recurrent rates and explains the conditional independence qualification, so the figure remains a local count example.

High rates with zero slope do not distinguish neighboring values, so they contribute no local information. A sharply changing rate can be informative even if it is smaller than another cell's peak rate. The coordinate here describes the network's present internal state. It need not be a currently visible external stimulus. Sensory Fisher information has the same Poisson formula only when the stimulus dependent tuning curves are the relevant rates.

Adding baseline firing raises the count noise without changing the slope, reducing local information. These are illustrative tuning curves, not recorded neurons or a demonstrated attractor network.
